A novel approach, referred to as reward-biased maximum likelihood estimation (RBMLE), addresses the issue of slow convergence in adaptive control by introducing a bias towards the optimal reward function. This method is further analyzed through a large-deviation analysis to determine its convergence properties in the adaptive control setting. The results of the study are then applied to a practical scenario, specifically the adaptive feedback control of a Rayleigh duct damping system. The findings of the research indicate that RBMLE outperforms existing convergence bounds in adaptive control by a factor of several orders of magnitude, leading to promising prospects for real-world implementation. The study also highlights potential areas for further investigation. This work is part of an ongoing series on the subject and will be followed up with additional experiments and case studies in future publications. We propose a new dataset, Lecture2Dub, consisting of 100 publicly accessible lectures accompanied by their corresponding subtitles. To leverage this dataset, we developed an end-toend system capable of generating video lectures in response to text inputs. This system is comprised of a multimodal encoder-decoder transformer paired with a text-to-voice synthesis model. Utilizing this setup, we investigated two approaches to generating video presentations: one that integrates both text and visual elements, and another that transforms spoken dialogue into a synthesized speech. Experimental results indicate that the system producing synthesized speech yields better outcomes, and further evaluations reveal that multimodal presentations lead to enhanced comprehension. To support our findings, we conducted a user study and compared the effectiveness of text, audio, and visual modalities. Finally, we conducted a large-scale evaluation by having users complete knowledge quizzes under both traditional and multimedia conditions, and the results demonstrate that multimodal presentations significantly enhance knowledge transfer. To facilitate further research, our dataset, code, and generated video lectures are now publicly available. For more information, please visit https://lectures-to-dub.github.io. Recent advancements in large transformer-based language models have enabled the calculation of surprisal estimates for human-like parsing tasks, mirroring reading time data. We examine the applicability of this approach to analyzing reading times for specific linguistic elements, such as the fixation times on named entities in human comprehension. We evaluate the concordance between surprisal estimates and fixation times for a set of 239 named entities extracted from the GPT-2 model, finding that larger models tend to overestimate named entity reading times compared to actual human data. We discover that the GPT-2 model incorrectly predicts the order of word fixation for certain entities, which can be attributed to the model's tendency to produce repetitive names. We also observe that the overestimation is more pronounced for less frequent entities, possibly due to the model's underutilization. We discuss potential causes of this discrepancy and suggest avenues for improving the accuracy of surprisal estimates. We also propose a straightforward method to adjust the surprisal estimates for less frequent items, thereby enhancing their alignment with human data. The analysis contributes to a deeper understanding of the strengths and limitations of surprisal estimates as a proxy for human parsing performance. We release our code and data set on GitHub, making it possible to replicate our study in the future. The data set is particularly valuable for researchers working on studies related to natural language processing and human-computer interaction. We also make our pre-trained model available on the HuggingFace model hub. We believe that this study can serve as a foundation for future investigations into the limitations and potential of surprisal analysis in understanding human parsing performance. We also recommend that future studies explore the application of surprisal analysis to other parsing tasks, such as the comprehension of syntactic structures. Ultimately, our work highlights the potential for using large language models to model human parsing performance, but also underscores the need for continued development of more accurate and reliable analytical tools. We believe that the concordance between surprisal analysis and human parsing data can be strengthened through the development of more sophisticated analysis techniques. We propose that future studies should focus on developing more precise and reliable surprisal analysis methods, which can better capture the complexities of human parsing performance. We also suggest that the development of more sophisticated analysis techniques can also facilitate the creation of more accurate and informative models of human language processing. The rapid evolution of advanced, stealthy hacking techniques poses significant challenges to the development of effective countermeasures. To address this issue, we employ an innovative approach combining network traffic capture, graph theory, and machine learning algorithms. By utilizing a graph neural network trained on a dataset of labeled network traffic packets, we are able to identify and detect malicious network traffic. Through rigorous testing, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to established machine learning methods, including convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks. Furthermore, our approach offers the advantage of automatically generating labels for the model's representation of network traffic patterns, thereby facilitating the creation of more accurate and reliable models. Ultimately, our method is designed to be integrated into real-world network traffic monitoring systems, providing valuable insights and anomaly detection capabilities. Training neural networks on lengthy datasets proves to be challenging, as they're frequently divided into shorter sequences and combined in various orders to create a new dataset for model training. This study introduces "Skip-Sideways," a novel approach that enables models to directly learn from extremely long, real-world datasets without requiring them to be split into shorter segments. The method involves training a model by randomly selecting short sequence pairs from the dataset, using the data points between these segments as a form of regularization to prevent the model from overfitting. This results in a model that can be trained using significantly longer datasets than traditional methods, leading to improved performance. The effectiveness of Skip-Sideways is demonstrated through its application to several real-world datasets, including speech, text, and visual recognition tasks. The findings indicate that Skip-Sideways outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art results in speech and visual recognition tasks, while matching or surpassing the performance of other methods in text-based tasks. Additionally, the approach is shown to be compatible with both fully connected and transformer-based models, and can be applied to various tasks, including classification, regression, and density estimation. We introduce the aDaptive Accept RejecT (DART) method, a novel algorithm designed to solve complex stochastic multi-armed bandit problems involving multiple agents. DART is a dynamic approach that allows arm selection based on the current distribution of the arms, rather than fixed and known distributions. By leveraging a stochastic game model and incorporating a robust Viterbi-like algorithm, DART accurately determines the arm with the highest expected reward. Using DART, we develop a dynamic strategy for a team of agents to maximize their cumulative reward in a competitive environment. Our approach is demonstrated to achieve optimal results through both theoretical analysis and extensive simulations. Additionally, we showcase the effectiveness of DART by applying it to a challenging problem, where agents must identify the distribution of a Gaussian process characterized by unknown mean and variance. The results confirm that DART outperforms traditional methods in a variety of scenarios. This research is part of an ongoing project that aims to establish a new paradigm for solving stochastic multi-agent decision-making problems. A significant drawback of abstractive summarization systems is their propensity
to introduce inaccuracies in both the content and facts they generate. To address
this limitation, we propose an approach that leverages fact-checking resources to
evaluate the credibility of summaries. Our method integrates a summary generator
with a fact-checker, utilizing a BERT-based architecture to determine reliable
information. The fact-checker is trained to identify factual errors by comparing
model-generated summaries against a set of verified facts. When a summary
includes an inaccurately generated sentence, the BERT model identifies it as an
untrusted fact. To enhance performance, we incorporate a summary generator to
produce trustworthy summaries. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on
evaluating the veracity of summaries. Additionally, it outperforms existing
summaries in coherence and factuality. Our code and models are publicly available
for reproduction on our website. https://nlp.cs.technion.ac.il/~nlpresources/VerifiableSummaries.html.

The Semantic Web's Query Language, SPARQL, is widely applied in the field of Multimodal Question Answering Systems (MQASs). However, traditional SPARQL queries are limited in exploring implicit multimodal connections such as analogies and contradictions, which current MQASs heavily rely on. To address this, we introduce a novel approach combining SPARQL and the concept of "contextual fields" to facilitate implicit query generation. This method leverages data from multiple sources, including ontologies, knowledge graphs, and multimodal information to create contextual fields that enhance SPARQL's query generation capabilities. Additionally, we develop a method for generating SPARQL's union and optional clauses from these fields, which significantly improves the system's performance. To evaluate our proposed method, we conduct a comprehensive analysis on a large dataset of 11,000 questions and observe a notable improvement of 9.3% in answer retrieval. The ever-growing universe of available literature poses a significant challenge to contemporary scholarly search. Researchers are increasingly turning to semantic search, which enables them to express complex queries using natural language, thereby facilitating more accurate results. However, natural language queries can be ambiguous and may not effectively convey the desired meaning. To overcome this limitation, previous studies have employed query expansion as a means of improving search quality. The core idea behind query expansion is to identify semantically related documents that share similarities with the query, based on their co-occurrence in the literature. To this end, we introduce a novel query expansion framework that leverages the relationships between academic entities and their co-occurrence in the literature. Specifically, our framework utilizes a knowledge graph to identify entities that are relevant to the query and then employs a word embedding model to expand the query. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of scholarly search, which involved designing and training a query expansion system using a large corpus of academic papers. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art scholarly search methods, which rely on traditional IR techniques, such as BM25. Deep neural networks' effectiveness against adversarial attacks has been significantly enhanced through adversarial training, a robust approach that integrates attacks into regularized learning. However, this technique heavily relies on the strength and effectiveness of the attack generator. To address this, we present a novel adversarial training method that utilizes a generative neural model, trained using the VampNet framework, to generate high-quality adversarial examples. By leveraging a conditional normalizing flow, our approach can model the adversarial distribution and synthesize perturbations that are both small and impactful. To further strengthen the adversarial training, we incorporate a discriminative model, trained to differentiate between original and adversarial samples, and combine it with a debiasing technique to ensure our generator doesn't learn from discriminative patterns. Extensive experimentation on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet datasets demonstrates our approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods across various attack scenarios. Additionally, our analysis reveals that our adversarial generator successfully learns to model the adversarial distribution and highlights the benefits of combining it with a discriminative model. Multi-view reconstruction in 2D object detection is a challenge that has been overlooked in research. Current approaches to 3D object detection have primarily focused on the 2D level, neglecting the vertical aspect of objects in their transformations, which results in inaccurate projections and a significant decrease in performance when their transformations are applied to multi-view data. To address this limitation, we propose a new method, called Free3D, that incorporates 3D transformations into multi-view detection, allowing for more accurate and robust object proposals. By utilizing a 3D prior, our method can generate object proposals that are consistent across different views and can be evaluated in three dimensions. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the KITTI multi-view dataset, outperforming existing methods in terms of accuracy. Additionally, our method's ability to accurately detect objects in the vertical dimension highlights the importance of the vertical aspect in multi-view detection. Deep learning techniques have significantly improved the quantification of left ventricles in cardiac imaging, but many existing methods struggle to maintain their performance when applied to new datasets. This lack of generalization is particularly evident in scenarios where datasets from different hospitals are combined, where performance drops by 20% or more. This research investigates the use of the steerable pyramid transform (SPT) as a solution to this problem, which breaks down images into multiple frequency channels and allows for more effective multi-channel learning. We demonstrate that SPT-based methods can achieve comparable accuracy to full-resolution models while requiring significantly less data, and that they outperform these models when transferred to new datasets, resulting in a 3 to 16 fold improvement in generalization performance. This suggests that SPT-based models are a promising direction for accurate and robust left ventricle quantification. The rapid advancement of computer vision techniques has led to the successful application of deep learning in image-based bird species classification. Nevertheless, the process of training a deep learning model for bird classification is resource-intensive and requires significant expertise. Furthermore, collecting large datasets for specific bird species can be time-consuming and laborious. In order to address these challenges, this study proposes a transfer learning approach. It leverages the existing knowledge gained from a pre-trained model on a vast dataset of ImageNet images, and adapts it for bird species classification using a limited dataset. The approach is demonstrated through the development of two bird classification systems, namely BIRD-CLASS and BIRD-CLASS-2, which utilize the ImageNet pre-trained model. The BIRD-CLASS system focuses on classifying images into one of the 200 ImageNet classes, whereas the BIRD-CLASS-2 system is tailored for the specific classification of bird species. The BIRD-CLASS-2 system is further enhanced through the incorporation of a unique feature extraction technique, which combines the strengths of the pre-trained model's weights with a Convolutional Neural Network. The BIRD-CLASS-2 system is evaluated on a bird classification dataset comprising 12 species and demonstrates superior performance compared to the BIRD-CLASS system. The results indicate that the BIRD-CLASS-2 system achieves an average accuracy of 92.5% compared to the BIRD-CLASS system's average accuracy of 89.5%. Recent years have seen significant advancements in representation learning for graphs, with the goal of identifying meaningful patterns in network structures. However, most existing research has been limited to a single network, neglecting the rich information present in complex, multi-layer networks. To address this gap, we introduce a novel framework for learning representations from multi-layer networks. Our approach, which we call GeoSpec, draws on the success of graph neural networks and incorporates geometric principles to capture the unique patterns present in each layer. By fusing these geometric representations, we are able to extract a unified understanding of the network's structural and semantic features. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our method, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, GeoSpec also offers a straightforward mechanism for interpreting results, enabling a deeper understanding of the network's structural characteristics. Our research is the first to integrate geometric and semantic information across multiple layers, paving the way for new research directions in network analysis. However, their parallelization comes with a drawback - the need for synchronization, which has been a significant challenge in their parallelization, particularly when using the successive cancellation list (SCL) decoder. To address this issue, this research presents a new SCL algorithm that achieves synchronization without the need for additional processing or memory. The proposed algorithm relies on a serial decoder that sets a reference state and uses it to synchronize the parallel SC decoders, allowing them to resume the decoding process. As a result, this approach enables efficient parallelization of the SCL decoder and provides notable gains in decoding latency and throughput for diverse devices, ranging from smartphones to servers. Specifically, for 1024 and 10240 information bits, the latency reduction achieved by the proposed method is 18.5% and 47.5% respectively, in comparison to the conventional approach. Domain generalization, a key transfer learning method, is widely applied across various fields. Despite its extensive use, the underlying mechanisms of this approach remain poorly understood, particularly in terms of theoretical foundations. This study delves into the theoretical aspects of domain generalization, focusing on the relationship between domain generalization and foundation models. We examine the notion of foundation models, which leverage generalizability in large-scale foundation models to address domain generalization. This paper investigates the theoretical connections between foundation models and domain generalization, revealing that foundation models can effectively tackle domain generalization by learning a shared feature space. This shared space enables models to generalize well across domains, even when models are not explicitly designed for domain generalization. We also explore the challenges associated with foundation models, particularly in terms of robustness and fairness issues, which are crucial for their practical applications. Furthermore, this study discusses the future research directions for integrating foundation models with domain generalization. We hope that this work will stimulate further investigation into the intersection of these two areas, ultimately contributing to the development of more robust and generalizable domain generalizable foundation models. We also believe that this work will pave the way for the establishment of a new research branch that combines foundation models and domain generalization. A novel full-reference image quality metric, referred to as HDR-MSSIM, has been developed to evaluate the quality of images that have undergone HEVC-based HDR compression. HDR-MSSIM assesses three key aspects of HDR content: the structural integrity, spatial, and color information, in addition to the range of pixel values available. To validate the effectiveness of HDR-MSSIM, the metric was applied to a range of HEVC-based HDR compression databases, including the HDR-VTV, Vidyo, and Multi-view Vidyo databases. A new approach to single image dehazing algorithms has emerged, which combines data-driven and model-based techniques. The key advantage of model-based methods is their ability to handle complex hazy conditions, however they often struggle with capturing the detailed structure of clear scenes. On the other hand, data-driven methods can produce realistic results but often rely on assumptions that may not apply in various hazy conditions. To address this, we introduce a model-based data-driven dehazing algorithm that leverages a multi-layer perceptron to estimate transmission and atmospheric scattering parameters. The algorithm also incorporates a multi-stage transmission estimation process, which involves a rough initial transmission estimation, followed by refinement through atmospheric scattering estimation, and finally an iterative refinement stage. Additionally, we propose a multi-layer scattering model that captures the detailed structure of objects and scenes. Our algorithm outperforms existing methods on various datasets, and the code and data are available online. The algorithm can be implemented efficiently on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and embedded systems. Our experiments demonstrate that the algorithm can achieve a 2x speedup while maintaining comparable image quality compared to state-of-the-art methods. This study investigates the feasibility of applying Machine Learning to colliders for identifying Dark Matter candidates across a broad spectrum of masses and various Dark Matter types. To achieve this, we created simulated event data for the LHC, featuring pairs of quarks or gluons decaying into pairs of W, Z, or photons, along with sub-jet pairs in association with missing energy. These simulations were then classified by Machine Learning models using multi-output Support Vector Machines. We introduce a novel method to evaluate the reliability of the Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation (TUR) in non-equilibrium scenarios. To test our approach, we apply it to a widely used model of active matter, the Vicsek model, in a non-equilibrium steady state. The results show that the TUR holds true in this regime, albeit with some discrepancies, and indicate that the TUR is more reliable when considering fluctuations in entropy rather than energy. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the TUR is valid across a broader range of system sizes in the non-equilibrium state, outperforming its accuracy in equilibrium conditions. Ultimately, our research resolves to a single, overarching question: Can the Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation be universally applied across equilibrium and non-equilibrium systems? Our investigation aims to shed light on the fundamental principles governing the thermodynamics of fluctuation. To overcome this issue, we introduce a novel framework that leverages the fact that test datasets are often composed of data points that can be described by simpler underlying distributions, allowing for more effective generalization. This framework, referred to as Simple Data for Simple Tasks (SDST), involves dividing test data into subsets based on their complexity and learning models using the easier subsets while making test-time predictions on the more complex samples within each subset. We theoretically analyze the generalization performance of SDST and provide conditions under which it can achieve near-optimal results, as well as establish a risk bound for SDST in TWA. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence to support our findings and show that SDST can significantly improve generalization performance in various deep learning tasks. Additionally, we explore the challenges of identifying simple datasets in practice and propose a practical approach to estimate them effectively. Our results indicate that SDST can achieve substantial generalization improvements in deep learning, with up to a 20% reduction in test error. This research paper presents an innovative algorithm for financial time-series clustering into distinct market periods using an enhanced version of the $k$-nearest neighbors method. By leveraging an advanced machine learning technique, this approach effectively identifies the closest data points within a specified distance threshold, thus determining the most suitable market periods. Our method, tailored for use with financial time-series, utilizes a modified distance metric to capture market regime characteristics. By applying this approach to S&P 500 index time-series, we were able to identify the patterns of market volatility resulting from the 2008 financial crisis. Additionally, this approach provides an effective method for analyzing the relationships between market periods and specific economic events, and enables the identification of their respective effects. By combining our algorithm with a decision tree, we were able to develop an early warning system for predicting market crashes. Our results demonstrate the superiority of this approach over existing methods for financial time-series analysis. Finally, we discuss the practical applications of our algorithm in real-world scenarios. Effective infectious disease surveillance is crucial for tracking and controlling outbreaks.  Non-specific syndromic surveillance involves analyzing reported health data to identify potential threats, without relying on confirmed case data.  A key challenge in this field is developing algorithms that can learn from imperfect data sources, including missing information and unobserved cases.  Our research introduces an innovative learning approach, called the Multi-Perspective Ensemble, which combines evidence from various sources to accurately detect outbreaks.  We evaluated this method using a large dataset from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, comparing its performance to established techniques such as the ProbaTrend and ProbaPost algorithms.  Our results demonstrate that the Multi-Perspective Ensemble outperforms existing methods, providing more accurate outbreak predictions and higher detection rates, particularly for smaller outbreaks.  Moreover, our findings show that the Multi-Perspective Ensemble is a robust and reliable approach, capable of handling missing data and unobserved cases.  We believe that this method can significantly contribute to more effective and timely infectious disease surveillance.  Our code is publicly available, providing an opportunity for researchers to replicate and build upon our work.  Our goal is to facilitate collaboration and knowledge-sharing in this field. Handwritten text recognition (HTR) research has seen significant advances with the adoption of recurrent and convolutional neural networks. However, a critical challenge remains in effectively processing large documents containing various types of information such as historical accounts, letters, and dates. To overcome this hurdle, a novel approach called the Date-First model has been proposed. This method leverages a simple architecture combining a convolutional neural network and long short-term memory model to accurately identify and extract handwritten dates from documents. A key component of the Date-First model is an object detection system that identifies potential dates in a given image, and feeds the output as input to an HTR system. Our Date-First model significantly outperforms existing date recognition models, boasting a character error rate reduction of 50.0% compared to the best baseline on a well-established benchmark. Moreover, a character error rate of 0.764 was achieved, marking a notable improvement over the state-of-the-art. Our proposed Date-First model also exhibits efficiency in both processing time and memory usage. Additionally, a character error rate of 0.909 was achieved on a real-world date dataset, underscoring its practical applications in the field. Building on the success of self-supervised learning, we introduce a novel method called Contrastive Domain Adaptation (CDA) that enhances domain adaptation by incorporating contrastive domain alignment. CDA's key feature is a contrastive loss function that aligns domain-specific features within a disentangled latent space. This approach enables the model to capture domain-specific information while maintaining consistency across domains. CDA's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on multiple benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we apply CDA to the task of medical image segmentation and achieve superior results when compared to existing domain adaptation methods. The code for CDA is publicly available at https://github.com/kaust-srai/CDA. When applied to the segmentation of the colon and pancreas, our method outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques. Machine listening tasks such as audio segmentation and sound event detection aim to identify segments of audio and corresponding events within an audio file.  However, most current methods rely on a single audio feature and may struggle with detecting rare or unusual sound events.  To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel method that leverages both visual and audio source information to enhance audio event detection.  By incorporating audio input and processing it using multiple layers, we first identify potential sound events and then use a unique attention mechanism to highlight relevant audio features associated with these events.  Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, with notable improvements over previous methods on standard benchmark datasets, particularly for detecting rare and unusual sound events.  Furthermore, our method outperforms other top-performing techniques, according to the Sound Event Detection Task at the 2020 DCASE challenge. This research investigates the privacy-utility tradeoff in a specific adversarial learning model that adheres to either one of two privacy constraints. The first constraint is derived from a widely accepted statistical definition of privacy, while the second is based on an alternative, more relaxed notion of privacy that prioritizes the confidentiality of individual measurements rather than joint measurements. We develop two privacy-utility tradeoff analyses for these settings and demonstrate that the proposed results surpass previously established bounds, notably those developed by Kairouz et al. in 2019 and Wu et al. in 2021. The key to our generalization is the identification of a previously underexplored connection between statistical privacy and the concept of random-coding exponent from information theory. Additionally, this connection enables us to devise a novel privacy-utility tradeoff analysis for the alternative privacy setting, which is not previously explored in the literature. We further extend our generalization to a specific scenario where the data is distributed across multiple servers and the aggregation is performed locally. The proposed solutions are also shown to be asymptotically optimal. We also present a more practical solution for the same problem and evaluate its performance through numerical experiments. This method empowers robots with a dynamic sense of power and enables them to adapt to their environment by learning from interactions. Through a unique learning process, the robot develops a predictive model of its surroundings, using this insight to determine an efficient navigation policy that takes into account the dynamics of its environment. Experimental results, both in simulated and real-world scenarios, demonstrate the effectiveness of APF in promoting collaboration, with the robot learning to adapt to changing environments, including navigating through crowded areas with reduced human avoidance. Furthermore, the proposed approach is shown to be efficient, scalable, and compatible with real-time implementation. Additionally, the code and materials for this method are made publicly available for further research and development. To our knowledge, the APF is the first data-driven navigation strategy that empowers robots to effectively collaborate with humans in shared workspaces. This innovative method is expected to be a crucial component in the development of collaborative human-robot teams. This phenomenon, where localized fluctuations overcome barriers to create a more efficient communication pathway, is achieved by carefully placing these obstructions to minimize network delays. This process, applicable to both artificial and living systems of interconnected elements, provides insight into how large-scale networks can optimize information flow across space and time. Additionally, our research shows that the optimal placement of these interactions can be solved through a combination of optimization techniques and the analysis of network pathways, with the number of interactions required directly proportional to the square root of the difference in distance between starting and ending points. Finally, our findings highlight the potential for this approach to be adapted for various network models, such as directed and weighted graphs. This adaptation involves formulating an equivalent optimization problem based on the minimum time required for a signal to travel between specified nodes in a network. Notably, our research demonstrates that the optimal solution for these more complex networks can be derived from the solutions of the original facilitation problem. For self-driving vehicles to safely navigate complex urban environments, accurate 3D object detection is crucial. This paper presents a novel, autonomous perception system capable of identifying multiple relevant objects within 2D images, without requiring ground truth labels. The proposed system is based on a semi-supervised learning approach that leverages a combination of synthetic data and limited annotated real-world data to train a 3D object detector. The detector utilizes a 3D-YOLO model, which integrates 2D object proposals with 3D bounding box regression, to detect objects within 3D bounding boxes. The system's 3D-YOLO model is trained using a novel, iterative proposal generation process, where 3D bounding boxes are created from 2D object proposals, and the detector is updated based on 3D bounding box regression. The proposed system is tested on the KITTI dataset, achieving a high average precision of 65.4% in the moderate difficulty metric. The proposed approach is also evaluated on a more challenging dataset, Cityscapes, and achieves an average precision of 63.1%. This study introduces a novel, end-to-end neural network called ParaNet, which directly processes 3D point clouds. Unlike conventional methods that rely on multi-view projections or voxelization to simplify inputs, ParaNet operates directly on raw point clouds. Their previous work, GeoNet, achieved state-of-the-art performance on 3D semantic segmentation but required supplementary projection modules. This study builds upon GeoNet by proposing a more efficient, end-to-end ParaNet, which replaces its projection modules with a voxelization module that uses a voxel grid filter to convert point clouds into simplified, voxelized representations. These representations are then processed by a 2D image-based neural network to produce accurate 3D semantic segmentations. The proposed ParaNet architecture combines a voxelization module with a novel, end-to-end network design, resulting in a significant reduction in parameters and improved efficiency. This design enables real-time, end-to-end training and inference, achieving state-of-the-art performance on semantic segmentation benchmarks. The proposed method is also demonstrated on a real-world, autonomous driving dataset, where it achieves superior results compared to other 2D-based 3D semantic segmentation methods. Speech recognition systems for low-resource languages often face significant challenges due to limited data availability. To address this issue, researchers have developed data enhancement methods, such as in- and out-domain synthesis, to supplement existing speech corpora. However, current methods are limited in their ability to generate diverse training data, resulting in poor model performance on actual unseen test data. To overcome this shortcoming, we propose an innovative approach that leverages background noise from an unrelated language to simulate speech in the target language, effectively transforming the problem into an adversarial task. By employing a novel speech-to-speech translation framework, we can enhance the diversity of training data and improve the robustness of speech recognition models to unseen test data. Experimental results on low-resource languages demonstrate substantial gains in model accuracy, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our method shows remarkable resilience to extreme out-of-domain test data, reducing error rates by as much as 50%. The role of attention in shaping perception is multifaceted. Our research explores how attention is allocated to specific visual characteristics, such as shape, location, and color. We developed a model that uses a neural network to predict gaze direction in response to images. The model is trained using eye movement data from real-world objects and then applied to synthetic images of objects with varying characteristics. Our findings indicate that paying attention to shapes is crucial for distinguishing between similar objects, and that attention to location is also influenced by object characteristics. Notably, our model demonstrates that attention allocation can be effectively generalized to artificial scenarios, such as differentiating between various types of disks. Current state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods utilize a single
uncertainty threshold to reject unreliable targets during training, yet this
approach overlooks the complexities of the uncertainty distribution within the
data.  To address this limitation, we introduce Curriculum Pseudo Labeling
(CPL), a novel framework that adapts to the uncertainty distribution to
improve semi-supervised learning performance.  By dynamically adjusting the
uncertainty threshold, CPL ensures high accuracy pseudo labels for easy
samples and increased the coverage of labeled samples.  The training process
is optimized by a learned threshold schedule, and a hybrid loss function is
proposed to counteract pseudo label noise through energy-based models.  The
results of our experiments demonstrate superior performance of CPL over 5
baselines across various benchmark datasets for image classification.  The
implementation details and model demos are accessible via GitHub.

Using 1.0 fb^-1 of data from the LHCb experiment, we analyzed direct CP violation in D0 mesons as they decay into h- and h+ particles.  Specifically, we investigated three scenarios: semileptonic and hadronic decays, and all decays combined - each giving us separate insights into CP violation within the charm system.  Our analysis of the semileptonic decays yielded an average CP violation parameter of -0.44 (or +0.48) with an error margin of 0.60.  For the hadronic decays, we found a separate average CP violation parameter of +0.19 (or -0.19) with an error margin of 0.58, while combining all methods resulted in an average CP violation parameter of +0.22 (or -0.22) with an error margin of 0.36.  Our findings align with Standard Model predictions and provide the most precise measurement of CP violation in the charm system to date.  Moreover, we found no evidence of CP violation in any of the scenarios with a probability of 83%, 70%, or 77% respectively.  As a result, we placed the tightest constraint yet on CP violation in the charm system. Federated learning, a decentralized technique, enables training of machine learning models on multiple devices without central data storage. Personalized FL further refines this concept by allowing each device to fine-tune its model towards its specific needs, as it has locally gathered data. However, this approach often leads to inconsistent model parameters across devices, hindering performance. To address this, we propose an innovative method, FL-HN, that leverages hypernetworks to personalize FL models. By using a single global model and generating device-specific models, FL-HN effectively adapts to diverse data distributions. Additionally, FL-HN incorporates a novel hypernetwork weight transfer mechanism, enabling efficient communication and reducing model storage. Experimental results demonstrate FL-HN's superiority over current personalized FL benchmarks, showcasing its ability to achieve better accuracy and reduce communication costs. Moreover, FL-HN's computational efficiency and robustness against model attacks have been successfully validated. Pre-trained multilingual language models have achieved significant success in cross-lingual tasks by leveraging their ability to transfer knowledge from high-level representations to other languages. Our research investigates the transfer of semantic meaning in multilingual BERT (mBERT) across languages, revealing that its output embeddings contain language-specific and language-independent information. These results shed new light on the transfer of semantic meaning in cross-lingual tasks and the inner workings of pre-trained language models. Additionally, the findings from this study can inform the design of model architectures to improve performance in downstream tasks. We present efficient algorithms for determining whether a directed graph is 
weakly connected or strongly connected along with finding its strongly connected 
components. These algorithms operate within a single pass through the adjacency 
matrix of the graph. For passing through the adjacency matrix just once, they 
produce the same partitioning of strongly connected groups as a standard linear 
time algorithm that leverages depth- or breadth-first search. An alternative 
approach involves two passes, resulting in a more refined grouping of strongly 
connected components. Our methods draw inspiration from linear algebra concepts, 
operating directly on the graph's Laplacian matrix, to identify and group strongly 
connected components. The key to these algorithms lies in the properties of the 
graph's eigenvalues and eigenvectors, derived from the Laplacian matrix. As a 
result, these algorithms can be applied to graphs where the eigenvalue distribution 
is known, regardless of their specific structure. This property makes our methods 
applicable to various types of graphs, including those generated by random processes 
such as the Erdős-Rényi model, the Barabási-Albert model, and the Watts-Strogatz model. 
Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these algorithms, resulting in 
a significant reduction in computational time compared to traditional eigenvalue 
computation methods. This efficiency enables the analysis of large graphs that would 
otherwise be unfeasible using standard techniques. The associated code is publicly

We introduce a new approach to mass mapping that leverages a trans-dimensional MCMC sampler. This technique generates a set of optimal mass models by exploring all possible combinations of parameters. These models are evaluated on a separate validation dataset, and the best fit is selected based on a measure such as mean squared error. In a simulation study, we found that our trans-dimensional method achieves significantly better results than a single model trained using k-nearest neighbors on a dataset with a similar structure. Additionally, our approach performs on par with a method that trains multiple models via random forest and selects the best one for estimation. A real-world example in the Virgo cosmology study demonstrates that our trans-dimensional method can produce more accurate weak lensing maps than a conventional modeling technique. Overall, our results suggest that trans-dimensional MCMC sampling can be an effective strategy for mass mapping that rivals traditional methods. This approach can be particularly beneficial when dealing with complex models, as it allows for efficient exploration of all possible parameter combinations. On the other hand, it falls short in terms of efficiency when dealing with simpler models. A code for the methods discussed in this research is available online at https://github.com/skowalsky1/transdimensional_mass_mapping. We also provide a new Python package called transdimensional_mass_mapping_gui, which allows users to apply the trans-dimensional MCMC method in a user-friendly interface. This code is available for download at https://github.com/skowalsky1/transdimensional_mass_mapping_gui. We plan to release the code under a permissive open-source license. Recent advances in generative adversarial networks (GANs) have significantly impacted the field of computer vision, particularly in image analysis and creation. While unsupervised GANs can produce high-quality images without guidance, they often struggle to meet specific requirements. Conversely, supervised GANs can be tailored to specific objectives but may require expensive and extensive training data. This paper proposes a novel, self-supervised approach to GANs that leverages images already present in a dataset to generate new, diverse images. Our method, built on the principles of self-supervised learning, relies on GANs to create synthetic images that effectively mask real images. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to a single-image deblurring task, which involves synthesizing images with various blur levels for network training, thereby eliminating the need for extensive dataset annotation. Our results show that this approach not only produces high-quality synthetic images but also effectively aids network training for the deblurring task. Furthermore, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the standard fastfhenz dataset, while our approach is also extended to other image creation tasks, such as image denoising and image compression, which yields promising results. Specifically, we examine how incorporating a basic task like counting the frequency of words can significantly enhance the robustness of language models, particularly in terms of accuracy and memory retention. Our findings indicate that this increased robustness stems from the positive impact on the model's weight distribution, which becomes more evenly balanced as the number of incorporated tasks increases. Notably, this benefit can be attributed to the model's need to allocate smaller amounts of weight to individual parameters in order to achieve the best results across multiple tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this increased robustness translates into improved resistance to minor hardware failures, as evidenced by our experiments using the NeuroSPADE hardware fault injection tool. Our results show that language models trained on multiple tasks can maintain their accuracy at a much higher rate than models trained on a single task, particularly when subjected to significant levels of hardware failure. For instance, a model trained on 4 tasks retained 90% of its accuracy after injecting 10% of its neuron faults, whereas a model trained on a single task retained only 50% after the same level of fault injection. These findings underscore the potential benefits of incorporating multiple tasks into language model training in terms of enhancing their resilience to hardware failures. As a result, this approach has important implications for the development of robust and reliable language models that can withstand minor hardware failures. This research investigates a smart meter network with distributed data transmission capabilities through a multi-channel, multi-access wireless random access model. Furthermore, the reinforcement learning implementation yields faster convergence than the queue proportion rule and achieves lower waiting times as the number of smart meters increases. However, our model may have a higher training time compared to the simple queue proportion rule. The rapid growth of Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices has raised significant privacy concerns, as personal and sensitive information is collected and transmitted to cloud or edge servers. A potential solution to mitigate these concerns is to implement data processing on the device itself, but this approach is hindered by limited computational and energy resources. A novel framework has been proposed that strikes a balance between processing on the device and off-device computing while ensuring privacy preservation. This framework involves a joint optimization of device and server processing, and a block-based processing architecture that maximizes off-device processing without compromising privacy. A two-stage optimization approach is used to solve the resulting complex problem, and it is evaluated through simulations of real-world IoT applications, showcasing substantial offloading gains and reduced processing time compared to traditional methods. Moreover, the proposed framework achieves a 2-6 fold reduction in energy consumption for device processing, and up to 32% reduction in server energy consumption compared to a baseline approach. A detailed analysis of the impact of various parameters on the framework's performance is also presented. Finally, the results of this study demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework to significantly improve the energy and latency efficiency of IoT-based systems, and enhance the overall quality of experience for IoT users. This study examines the Gelfand-Kirillov dimension of Leavitt path algebras $A_{\Lambda}$ derived from row-finite higher Leavitt paths. Key findings indicate that the G-K dimension of $A_{\Lambda}$ is equal to $n+1$ if the Leavitt path contains $n$ loops and no infinite orbits. Moreover, the G-K dimension of $A_{\Lambda}$ is at most $n+1$ if the number of infinite orbits in the Leavitt path is zero or one. The relationship between the G-K dimension of $A_{\Lambda}$ and the G-K dimensions of the associated unitization $A^+(V_{\Lambda},\phi)$ is also investigated. Notably, if the Leavitt path contains no infinite orbits, the G-K dimension of $A^+(V_{\Lambda},\phi)$ equals that of $A_{\Lambda}$. However, when the Leavitt path has one infinite orbit, the G-K dimension of $A^+(V_{\Lambda},\phi)$ surpasses that of $A_{\Lambda}$. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the G-K dimension of the higher Leavitt path algebras $A_{\Lambda_1 \Lambda_2 \ldots \Lambda_n}$ and $A^+(V_{\Lambda_1 \Lambda_2 \ldots \Lambda_n}, \phi)$ are both $n+1$ when the higher Leavitt path contains $n$ loops and no infinite orbits. The study also explores the relationship between the G-K dimension of the higher Leavitt path algebras and their unitizations. The results presented in this paper extend previously established findings regarding Leavitt path algebras by Xun Liu and Xiao-Qing Zheng. This research introduces a novel approach to text generation using language models, which leverages a technique known as LST (Label Smoothing Transformer). By generating multiple potential text sequences in a single forward pass, this method can efficiently produce more authentic language outputs. Our study demonstrates that when combined with a small autoregressive decoder, LST can produce text with comparable quality to a top language model. Moreover, this method can seamlessly integrate with existing sampling methods, leading to enhanced results in both reference generation and conditional tasks such as paraphrasing. Through both automated and human evaluations, we found that LST can outperform or match the performance of leading language models, particularly when generating text with greater linguistic coherence. Furthermore, our method can process longer sequences in real-time without requiring any architectural modifications, making it suitable for use in interactive applications. This process bears similarities to those found in normal fluids, particularly in regards to self-similar solutions. This discrepancy arises from the differing time scales associated with electron motion and plasma pressure gradient response. As a result, plasma shock waves exhibit an additional degree of freedom, allowing for an infinite number of independent self-similar solutions. As modern processors continue to accelerate, understanding the behavior of programs becomes increasingly complex due to the ease with which operations can be performed out of order. To address this, a novel approach called promising semantics is proposed, which provides a guarantee that operations can be reordered without affecting program correctness. The initial definition of promising semantics relies on a program analysis that identifies independent tasks, but this study presents a more efficient method. It demonstrates that promising semantics can be ensured by dividing programs into well-known patterns, such as sequence, selection, and loops, and applying a simplified analysis to each pattern. This research also introduces a new concept called pattern promisingness, which measures the complexity of program patterns, and discusses its implications for promising semantics application. The results show that pattern promisingness effectively identifies and ranks promising semantics feasibility in various programs. Additionally, this study presents a new language extension, called PromL, which provides a framework for promising semantics implementation. The PromL language leverages pattern promisingness to automatically determine promising semantics applicability, and features a novel reordering rule to ensure the correctness of program reordering. The integration of PromL with promising semantics has been successfully tested across various benchmarks, including those from the CompCert C compiler and the JavaCard API. The results demonstrate the potential of promising semantics to improve program performance while maintaining correctness. The complete implementation of PromL is publicly available.

This research focuses on developing an integrated control strategy for a complex system comprising multiple interconnected sub-systems. We employ Model-Predictive Control (MPC), which relies on an internal model to simulate the system's behavior and ensure stability and performance. However, when the sub-systems change, the internal model becomes outdated and requires recalibration. To address this, we propose an innovative online learning method that leverages the sub-systems' interactions and information to update the internal model in real-time. By combining the MPC's control signal with the sub-systems' observations, our approach identifies the optimal model parameters and achieves stability. We demonstrate the approach's effectiveness through simulations of a multi-robot system interacting with a crowd of robots. The results indicate that our method outperforms a standard MPC implementation and a more recent online learning technique. We also analyze the impact of various parameters and provide recommendations for their optimal tuning. Ultimately, this work showcases the potential of our approach in a real-world application involving a swarm of robots in a magnetic levitation experiment. We study the ground states of one-dimensional, non-self-adjoint Jacobi operators with quasi-periodic eigenvalue properties, supported by recent Hedenmalm-Skeppstedt and Lyubarsky type theories. The ground states' behavior, as the system size increases, is analyzed through the lens of a spatially distributed variable, characterized by a probability density function, akin to the ground state wavefunction in traditional approaches. The ground state's energy is analyzed as a distribution functional, balancing the potential energy with a kinetic energy component, and the existence of these states is demonstrated via a variational principle, building upon existing mathematical frameworks and generalizing some prior results to the case of non-self-adjoint operators. Additionally, we explore connections to the ground state problem in discrete, non-Hermitian Dirac operators with quasi-periodic dispersion relations. The findings are illustrated through numerical examples. A companion project involves a Python code that computes ground states in finite systems based on the distributed variable formulation and visualizes the associated potential energy and kinetic energy. Intent classification plays a crucial role in dialog system development. 
This process involves categorizing user utterances into distinct intent categories. 
For instance, in a food delivery dialog system, the user's intent might be to order food or inquire about the order status. 
To address the limitations of supervised learning in intent classification, 
multitask learning and semi-supervised learning methods have been proposed. 
However, these approaches have their own set of drawbacks. 
This paper presents a novel approach to intent classification, 
which leverages weakly supervised learning techniques. 
The proposed method involves generating weak labels from utterances, 
using a set of unlabeled utterances to select a subset of labels, 
and then training a model on both strong and weak labels. 
The experimental results on two publicly available datasets show that, 
in the context of weakly supervised learning, the proposed method performs on par with a fully supervised approach. 
The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub. 
A corresponding web application is also provided to facilitate further exploration of the method. 
The link to this application is available at https://intclassificationws.lsm.com.

This paper introduces a method to simulate and evaluate critical scenarios for collision avoidance, where a vehicle may collide with another or a pedestrian, utilizing a generative adversarial network (GAN). The proposed system, composed of two components, works in harmony to create and assess these critical scenarios. The first component, working in conjunction with a GAN, generates a set of scenarios from a distribution that represents real-world data. The second component, based on GAN equilibrium, assesses the scenarios to determine if they indeed fit within this distribution. The proposed system's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on a simulated environment, involving a self-driving vehicle navigating urban roads. The results show that the vehicle is rarely exposed to scenarios that do not occur in reality, and the scenarios generated are realistic, with the system successfully identifying and simulating real-world scenarios approximately 90% of the time. The integration of variable energy sources into the power system poses significant challenges to grid stability and operator control, particularly due to the uncertainty of energy production. To address this issue, we propose a real-time prediction tool that forecasts solar power generation. Leveraging advanced machine learning techniques, our predictive model combines historical solar data with weather forecasts to generate accurate, short-term predictions. We tested our model using historical solar observations and detailed weather conditions from the US weather monitoring network, achieving a notable mean absolute error per prediction of less than 0.4 megawatts, within a 3-hour forecasting horizon. This breakthrough could enable more effective management of variable power sources and contribute to improved grid stability. Our predictive model, built using a random forest algorithm, is capable of processing vast datasets and providing reliable, near-real-time forecasts. These forecasts can be easily integrated into existing control systems, enabling power operators to quickly respond to changes in the power grid. Additionally, our model's ability to generate reliable forecasts at a high resolution can be applied to other weather forecasting scenarios, where accurate predictions are crucial for decision-making. We believe that our predictive model represents a significant step towards developing a more reliable and resilient power grid. We have made our dataset and code publicly available for further research and analysis. We establish a level set formula for divergence-form elliptic operators with symmetric concave functions, under partial uniform ellipticity conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the weak Harnack principle holds for solutions to the associated degenerate equation. Additionally, in the context of quadratic functions, we investigate the structure of level set boundaries and the connected components within each region defined by $\{u_\pm\geq 0\}$, where $u$ is a solution. Specifically, for $n\geq2$, we prove that any two connected components are conical in nature. Notably, this result extends a previous finding by Scheffer for the special case of $n=2$ and $f(x)=|x|^2$. Our proof draws upon a combination of techniques, including level set flow methods, topological analysis, and the degenerate case study of Li-Schoen regarding level set flows of degenerate elliptic operators. In contrast to existing approaches for conical self-congruence, our method does not rely on the assumption of $C^2$ regularity, instead leveraging the degenerate case study of Kiselev-Sire-Serrin. Moreover, our work also encompasses an alternative proof of the conical structure theorem for level sets of the $p$-Laplacian in the special case where $p=n$. We've analyzed the dynamic properties of the Fredrickson-Andersen model, a type of random lattice gas with kinetic constraints, and its behavior under self-consistent dynamics. By deriving a set of mean field equations, we investigated the model's phase structure and compared our findings with numerical simulations conducted on a 3D cubic lattice. Our results indicate good agreement between the self-consistent analysis and numerical data. We also explored the model's dynamics on shorter timescales and identified key features of its relaxation behavior. Furthermore, we examined the model's behavior under conditions where particles can temporarily occupy more than their allotted sites, and found that this leads to a more complex phase structure with distinct metastable states. A detailed analysis of the model's phase structure and dynamic properties is provided, along with a discussion of the implications of our findings. Finally, we discuss the broader applications of the Fredrickson-Andersen model in the context of glassy dynamics. This research draws heavily from the author's master's thesis, a comprehensive study that includes additional results and visualizations not presented in this work. This research focuses on improving monocular 3D object detection by leveraging depth information generated from a depth estimator. We examine the impact of different depth estimation methods on the performance of monocular 3D detectors and identify key challenges associated with current monocular 3D detectors. To address these issues, we introduce a novel 3D detector called Mono3D+, which is an optimized version of the traditional 3D detector. Mono3D+ enhances the monocular 3D detector by employing a multi-task learning approach, which trains the detector to predict depth and 3D bounding box parameters simultaneously. Additionally, we introduce a novel loss function that combines classification loss, regression loss, and depth loss to improve overall performance. Experimental results on the KITTI dataset demonstrate that Mono3D+ outperforms the baseline 3D detector and other state-of-the-art methods in 3D detection tasks. The accompanying code and model weights will be publicly available upon paper acceptance. Our method is also adaptable to other monocular 3D detectors, and we expect it to achieve comparable results on other datasets. We present a method for generating controllers that operate in the world model to replicate a desired behavior within the actual world. Building on a verified controller synthesis approach, this technique leverages a planner that synthesizes control in the world model, utilizing a PDDL [1] planner for trajectory planning. In this study, we explore integrating PDDL planners with model checking techniques, specifically using Temporal Model Checking on world models to verify planned trajectories and ensure safety. A key aspect of this approach involves translating temporal properties into PDDL, enabling the creation of invariant and goal states in the model, thus facilitating synthesised trajectory validation. Notably, this technique is capable of guaranteeing safe trajectories for complex systems, such as multi-rotor vehicles. Furthermore, it is highly adaptable, allowing seamless integration with various world models and planning algorithms. A notable advantage lies in its ability to incorporate temporal properties, a feature that is often overlooked in traditional verified controller synthesis approaches. By integrating model checking and verified controller synthesis, this technique offers a comprehensive framework for generating safe trajectories in complex environments. A comprehensive implementation is provided using the Open Motion Planning Library (OMPL) and PDDL planner tools like LPOV3 and Minisat2, available at https://github.com/ArXivPublications/Temporal-Verified-Controller-Synthesis. A video demonstrating the results can be accessed at https://youtu.be/6ZT6z6z6z6. A companion blog post detailing the implementation is available at https://www.ompl.org/base/Temporal-Verified-Controller-Synthesis. Future work will focus on expanding this technique to accommodate stochastic world models. In this paper, we present a novel policy learning algorithm, referred to as the Fitted Emulator Actor-critic (FEAC) algorithm, designed to operate effectively in non-stationary settings. FEAC leverages a fitted Gaussian emulator to approximate the policy, complemented by a Q-function approximated using a deep neural network, both of which are learned through supervised learning techniques. Our algorithm, FEAC, is compared to a leading alternative, Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), through experiments involving robotic manipulation and locomotion tasks. Our results indicate that FEAC yields superior performance, achieved without compromising on sample efficiency, and we further analyze the properties of FEAC's policy, revealing its potential to generalize to novel scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate FEAC's capacity to adapt to non-stationary environments by continuously learning from new samples as they become available. Our findings suggest that FEAC presents a promising approach to policy learning, particularly in scenarios where sample efficiency and generalizability are paramount. Our system, Graphene, utilizes Open IE to convert text into structured knowledge graphs that represent relationships between concepts. Graphene's unique approach breaks down the complex Open IE task into two distinct subtasks. It first identifies and structures core elements within sentences, such as subjects, predicates, and objects, which form the foundational structure of the graph. Next, it applies a multi-task learning framework to semantically relate these elements across different sentences and refine the graph's structure. Our evaluation on a substantial dataset demonstrates Graphene's effectiveness in extracting complex relationships, achieving a 22% or greater improvement over current benchmarks in representing simple and complex assertions. Furthermore, Graphene's ability to connect and integrate multi-sentence knowledge across documents significantly outperforms existing methods. The field of explainable AI is rapidly expanding, with researchers and industries alike recognizing its value in numerous applications. However, despite significant breakthroughs, a crucial aspect of explainable AI remains underexplored: the stability of model explanations. This oversight is particularly concerning in high-stakes environments, where inaccurate explanations can lead to devastating consequences. To address this gap, our study delves into the stability of local surrogate explanations, which remains an unsolved challenge despite recent advancements in global surrogate stability research. By developing a novel approach using random forests, we demonstrate that local surrogate stability can be achieved and that it significantly improves the accuracy of local interpretability metrics. Our findings also reveal that local surrogate stability is influenced by various factors, including the underlying model structure, the choice of feature subset, and the type of explanation used. This research has the potential to shed light on the stability of model explanations, enabling researchers to create more reliable and trustworthy models. The code and datasets used in this study are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhuyuan-github/stable-explanations. This research presents a novel technique for enhancing the direction of arrival (DOA) estimation of a target speaker in a noisy environment by utilizing an external microphone. Our proposed method involves transmitting a noise reference signal from the external microphone and modulating it into a wideband multipath signal through a sub-band channel estimator. To increase the accuracy of DOA estimation, we employ a target speaker separation network and a spatial prediction network. Our approach involves first using the external microphone to generate a noise reference signal, which is then transmitted to the target speaker through a noise reference network. This signal is modulated into a wideband multipath signal by a spatial domain channel estimator. Next, we apply a target speaker separation network to isolate the target speaker's signal and use a spatial prediction network to predict the target speaker's signal in the absence of noise. Our proposed method achieves significant improvements in DOA estimation performance in noisy environments, outpacing state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our noise reference transmission approach, showing that transmitting noise from the microphone has a negligible impact on the target speaker. Our research also explores the optimal noise reference transmission delay and power to minimize interference. Our proposed method has been successfully implemented on an FPGA and achieves DOA estimation speeds of up to 22.7 kHz. This technique has been successfully applied to a wireless communication system, enhancing the performance of beamforming and offering a potential solution for end-to-end speech recognition in multi-user environments. In a binary opinion formation model, agents' interactions on a social network result in a rapid opinion convergence due to the influence of majority opinions. Zealots, or stubborn agents, with fixed opinions, significantly slow this convergence and cause unusual opinion distributions to emerge. Focusing on networks with fixed degrees, we investigate opinion dynamics within a single-zealot network where degree is distributed according to a given distribution. Through a mathematical analysis, we precisely calculate the convergence time and the time-averaged opinion distribution of these networks. Our findings are further validated through numerical simulations. Notably, we also observe a phenomenon where extreme degree zealots can cause binary opinions to emerge in the network. Moreover, we demonstrate that these results can be extended to networks with multiple zealots, providing insights into how their interactions affect the network's characteristics. Additionally, we explore the network's time-averaged degree distribution and the emergence of a polarized opinion within it. Our study provides a framework to understand the impact of zealots on various social networks. The insights gained can be leveraged to develop strategies for influencing opinion dynamics in networks with zealots for targeted applications. Finally, we investigate the effects of zealot removal on these networks, revealing how removing a zealot can lead to the emergence of a polarized opinion and can potentially cause the network's opinions to shift towards the remaining zealot's opinion. Notably, we also observe that removing a zealot can lead to the emergence of a more extreme opinion than before. The findings of this study are supported by numerical simulations. We investigate the permeability of porous media through direct numerical simulation (DNS) and lattice Boltzmann methods (LBM) with specific attention to statistical fluctuations and accuracy. These computational techniques are compared in the context of evaluating permeability coefficients. To achieve this, we apply both DNS and LBM to the same porous media, employing a statistical approach to determine permeability coefficients. Our results demonstrate that LBM produces inaccurate permeability coefficients when certain Darcy laws are applied, particularly when statistical fluctuations are limited. Conversely, DNS yields accurate permeability coefficients that align with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we observe that increasing the size of the simulation domain does not significantly impact the accuracy of the LBM results, a finding that supports the use of LBM in permeability coefficient determination. To mitigate the inaccuracies of LBM, we propose an alternative approach that combines LBM with DNS, allowing for the accurate computation of permeability coefficients in porous media. Our results indicate that this hybrid approach produces accurate and reliable permeability coefficients for various porous media, solidifying the use of LBM in the simulation of porous media. Ultimately, our study provides a deeper understanding of the limitations and inaccuracies of LBM in the context of permeability coefficient determination. To this end, we recommend that researchers exercise caution when applying LBM to the simulation of porous media and consider the limitations of LBM in the face of statistical fluctuations and accuracy requirements. Our results are expected to provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners working in the simulation of porous media. This paper presents a pioneering study focusing on document type metadata in open access repositories, which has historically been an overlooked area of research. Our research aims to address this gap by analyzing the presence and quality of document type metadata within these repositories, as well as evaluating the impact of missing or inaccurate metadata on search accuracy. Our findings are based on a massive dataset extracted from Web of Science and Scopus, comprising over 187 million records. The results indicate a concerning trend of under-metadata reporting types, amounting to more than half of the total records. Notably, Scopus exhibits a higher proportion of missing metadata compared to Web of Science. Our experiments demonstrate that document type information can significantly enhance search performance, highlighting the importance of complete and accurate metadata for optimal search outcomes. The study's conclusions are grounded in empirical evidence and emphasize the practical implications of our findings. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of document type metadata and serves as a foundation for future investigations in this area. We introduce a Bayesian, probabilistic approach to autonomous vehicle tracking, focusing on updating beliefs about objects' identities. Probabilistic vehicle tracking methods often rely on sophisticated techniques, such as deep neural networks, Markov Switching models, or probabilistic object detectors. In contrast, our method is centered around a fundamental principle: reinforcing previously held beliefs, much like how humans retain information about objects' identities. We propose a two-stage system, where the first stage identifies objects within a scene and assigns identities, and the second stage iteratively updates and refines these identities. Through extensive testing on the NuScenes and Waymo Open dataset, our method outperforms current benchmarks, achieving 8.8% and 3.8% reductions in average displacement on NuScenes and Waymo respectively. Moreover, our method exhibits improved robustness in challenging scenarios, such as those with high numbers of objects or severe occlusions. We investigate the behavior of a magnetic vortex within a thin, magnetized disk exposed to a radio-frequency magnetic field. Through both numerical analysis and mathematical theory, we find that when the vortex is excited into a gyrotropic mode, it interacts strongly with nearby defects to create a persistent spin current flowing in a plane perpendicular to the magnetized disk and the vortex's axis. This process does not rely on the presence of electron spins or transport. Our research suggests that magnetic vortex states could serve as a unique source of spin defects. Additionally, we explore how the energy of the vortex's gyrotropic mode is affected by the size of the magnetized disk, finding that it can be described by the energy of a magnetic monopole. Finally, we propose that when the radio-frequency field is modulated, it could be possible to control the interactions between the vortex and defects, potentially allowing for the creation of new spin defects through spin pumping. This could have implications for the study of spin defects in materials with low spin-orbit coupling. However, pre-training models on Chinese video and language datasets is particularly challenging due to the complexity of multi-modal, event, and narrative semantics involved. To address this challenge, a pre-trained multi-modal model called DViMPro was developed using an enormous Chinese video and language dataset, totaling 1.2 billion. Comprehensive evaluations of DViMPro on these tasks in the CVT-1.5B and MSVD datasets reveal that DViMPro outperforms existing models, achieving a significant 26% improvement in video captioning, 10% in video question answering, and 9% in video retrieval. In the analysis of high-dimensional financial time series data, the use of vector autoregressive models is often hampered by the significant effects of data shrinkage. To address this issue, we explore the potential of Bayesian regularization techniques that promote sparsity in model coefficients. We specifically examine the application of two regularization methods: the first that employs a Student-t prior distribution to account for heavy-tailed distributions in returns, and a second method that combines multiple normal prior distributions on vector autoregressive model coefficients while maintaining a single mixture normal prior for residual variance. We propose a computational strategy for these approaches and conduct a thorough simulation study to evaluate their effectiveness across varying conditions, including different prior distributions, sample sizes, and dimensions. The results demonstrate the superior performance of the second method under a wide range of scenarios. We also apply these methods to a high-dimensional stock return data set and compare their performance with other prominent shrinkage estimators. The findings reveal that the second method outperforms the others in terms of forecasting accuracy, particularly during periods of extreme return fluctuations. Additionally, we investigate the effects of model misspecification on the accuracy of forecast error and risk estimates. The results suggest that the second method exhibits greater resilience to model misspecification across all considered metrics. Furthermore, we examine the characteristics of posterior distributions for autoregressive coefficients and residual variance under various prior settings, observing a notable sensitivity of the bivariate posterior distribution of autoregressive coefficients to prior specifications. The analysis also reveals that residual variance estimates tend to be more stable and less sensitive to prior specifications. The study's findings are supplemented by an empirical application to high-dimensional stock return data, which demonstrates the practical utility of the proposed methods.
